To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the prevalence of nocturnal blood pressure (BP) dipping in patients with hypertension and in the general population is high (around 70%) and is similar in men and women; (ii) in patients with hypertension, nocturnal BP dipping is associated with a reduced cardiovascular risk; (iii) in the general population, nocturnal BP dipper status is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events, but the risk is higher in non-dippers than in extreme non-dippers, and

1) nocturnal blood pressure reduction is greater for DBP (mean difference: 5.0 mmHg) than for SBP (mean difference 2.4 mmHg); 2) the difference between DBP and SBP is greater in patients than in normotensives (patients: 3.2 vs 1.8 mmHg); and 3) this difference increases in patients with a greater nocturnal blood pressure fall.
